entries.title: City lights up downtown Chicago with official Christmas tree at Millennium Park
entries.summary: <p>Millennium Park was packed with people craning to get a look at the 50-foot tree, as it flickered to life Friday evening along with a smattering of fireworks.</p><p>The City of Chicago's 113th annual tree lighting ceremony brought out the holiday spirit, along with a host of guests, including Grammy Award-winning artist Lalah Hathaway, Knott Us Band, Ballet Chicago performing "The Nutcracker," Joshua's Troop and even Santa Claus.</p><p>This year's Christmas tree was donated by the Clark family of Campton Hills.</p><p>Music from DJ Mike P kept the party going after the 6:25 p.m. tree lighting, playing crowd pleasers like “Party in the U.S.A.” and “Wobble.”</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson and Commissioner Kenya K. Merritt joined the events hosts, ABC7 Chicago’s Ryan Chiaverini and Val Warner, at the event. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure entries.title: 'It's like our living room': Montrose Saloon in Albany Park set to close after decades-long run
entries.summary: <p>All it took was one visit to Montrose Saloon for Brian Pudil, 65, and his wife to decide to move into the apartment next door. It was love at first drink.</p><p>Since then, and for the past 16 years, Pudil has gone to the bar about three or four times each week to connect with other Montrose regulars.</p><p>“It’s like our living room,” he said. “Most of us are very caring, intelligent people that are really community-minded and like to have fun”</p><p>After more than five decades, Montrose Saloon will close its doors after New Year’s Eve, the bar’s Facebook page announced Friday.</p><p>Pudil said some loyal patrons heard the news Thursday. One day later, hundreds of bar-goers and musicians flooded Montrose’s Facebook post with comments about their fond memories of and love for the venue.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> You’re in another world and just taken away from your everyday troubles,” Pudil said. “You’re in another dimension.”</p><p>The bar’s indoor space, covered with music albums and artists’ portraits, serves as a cozy spot for music lovers, while the bar’s outdoor patio operates as a family-friendly area, open to children and dogs.</p><p>According to the Saloon’s website, the Albany Park “bar on the corner” opened its doors in 1976, but those who know the bar best say Montrose has been around for decades longer.</p><p>“It opened in 1945 at least. entries.title: White Sox trade Jordan Leasure to Phillies, tender contract offers to four arbitration-eligible players
entries.summary: <p>As the deadline Friday to tender contract offers to arbitration-eligible players neared, the White Sox already had cleared out the two players who were on the bubble.</p><p>One of those players was reliever Jordan Leasure, who will miss all of next season while recovering from elbow surgery. Leasure was designated for assignment Thursday after right-hander Dustin May’s three-year, $52.5 million deal became official.</p><p>Nevertheless, the Sox found a trade partner, dealing Leasure to the Phillies for right-hander Christian Coppola, a 12th-round draft pick in July. Coppola isn’t a significant prospect at this point, but his intriguing slider eventually should find a home in the bullpen at Low-A Kannapolis.</p><p>The other was catcher Joey Bart, who was set to command an estimated $2.9 million salary in his final year of arbitration, according to MLB Trade Rumors. He was DFA’d Tuesday. The Sox needed a spot on their 40-man roster to add both infielder William Bergolla Jr. and left-hander Jaden Woods, and Bart was such an obvious candidate to depart that general manager Chris Getz openly discussed seeking a new backup catcher last week in Las Vegas.</p><p>The Sox acquired Bart in a trade in August, but his tenure with them was limited to three games by a wayward pitch that fractured a bone in his left hand. His stay in Chicago, however, will be longer. The Cubs claimed Bart off waivers Friday and agreed to terms with him on a contract for 2027.</p><p>The Sox tendered contract offers to third baseman Miguel Vargas, outfielder Brenton Doyle and relievers Huascar Brazoban and Chris Murphy, all of whom are arbitration-eligible for the first time.</p><p>The deadline for teams to agree on salaries with arbitration-eligible players normally is in mid-January, but that is likely to be delayed by a lockout.</p>

entries.title: Bulls' Caleb Wilson meets with media after hand surgery last week
entries.summary: <p>Playing “Grand Theft Auto VI” is a bit of a struggle with the brace on the right hand, but doable.</p><p>As far as when Caleb Wilson can leave Vice City and return to his full-time job as the face of the Bulls organization? The 20-year-old didn’t give a clear timetable but did make a promise.</p><p>“I’m trying to make sure my hand feels great,” Wilson said on Friday, speaking to the media for the first time since undergoing surgery last week to repair a broken hand. “I’m not going to come back and play if I feel like I’m not at my best because I’m not going to come back and be average.</p><p>“Taking it day by day, and I know in time it will feel better.”</p><p>Which should have the Bulls feeling better.</p><p>Before Wilson swiped at the basketball in Victor Wembanyama’s clutches and sustained the injury, he was everything a No. 4 overall pick in a loaded draft class was hyped up to be. The 6-foot-9 forward was averaging 18.9 points, 6.2 rebounds, and 1.8 steals per game, and learning under fire against the likes of New York, Philadelphia and Boston – two times each.</p><p>Now he’ll have to learn from the bench with street clothes on, as the original timetable released from the team was four-to-six weeks.</p><p>“A lot,” Bulls coach Tiago Splitter replied when asked what Wilson can take away from the team as a spectator. “How you react to everything, you see the struggles and also the enjoyment of just being with his teammates and going through the ups and downs of the game. I think that’s important. There are a lot of little things that happen during a game – small conversations, timeouts – a lot he can learn from.</p><p>“He’s a rookie, he just got here. It might be different if you’re a 15-year vet. He’s got to absorb everything he can to get better.”</p><p>Surprisingly, not a real stretch for Wilson. While his personality is that of a high-energy go-getter who expects greatness from himself, he had the game taken away from him last season at North Carolina when he broke his left hand and missed the NCAA Tournament run.</p><p>A hard lesson learned then.</p><p>This latest hand injury is a bit different in his eyes. It’s not season ending or close to it, and he knows that while there is no substitute to playing, there’s still a lot he can take away that he needs improvement in.</p><p>“It’s difficult, but it’s not long term,” Wilson said. “I’ll play again in a couple weeks, so I’m not really worried about it. It gives me an opportunity to get in shape more, see the game from a different view on the bench. I’m excited. I’m going to get stronger, I know what I need to get better at because I played against such great teams so early, so it’s exciting for me.”</p><p>Splitter hopes he does continue visually learning from a far and doing so in a suddenly winning culture. The Bulls went 3-1 in their first four games without Wilson, as Matas Buzelis has really stepped up in his absence.</p><p>That of course has led to the conspiracy theory that the Bulls – and specifically Buzelis – could somehow be better with Wilson short-term, and Splitter did his best to put that to rest.</p><p>“Two things: I think we are playing as a team better in terms of just getting used to what we need to do,” Splitter said. “Also, maybe Matas is having more touches now. It’s a matter of touches and confidence. I don’t think it is Matas is just playing good because Caleb is not here. When you have more touches, have the ball in your hands then naturally you’re going to have a chance to do more and feel good.”</p>

entries.title: Kam Buckner's concrete plans for House speaker
entries.summary: <p>I hate being wrong about things I’ve written. It can be horribly embarrassing.</p><p>But I actually kind of enjoy being wrong about private opinions I’ve formed that I haven’t actually shared with more than a few people. Gaining that extra bit of insight, which helps me set aside some notions that I had before, always feels like a victory to me.</p><p>And that brings us to state Rep. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fran-spielman-show/2026/11/11/kam-buckner-illinois-house-speaker-candidate-emanuel-chris-welch-ouster-harry-benton" >Kam Buckner</a>, D-Chicago. Buckner was named House speaker pro tempore by Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch, who recently <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/11/05/illinois-house-speaker-chris-welch-mutiny-26-democrats-call-for-new-leader-harry-benton-scandal" >announced</a> he would not seek another term after 27 of his members said they wouldn’t vote for him and it became apparent that several more held the same opinion.</p><p>Welch told me months ago that the appointment did indeed signal that Buckner was at least one of his favorites to replace him as the chamber’s leader. To me, that was a big strike against Buckner. Welch was one of now-imprisoned House Speaker Michael Madigan’s favorites, and I thought it unwise to repeat that formula this time around. A fresh start, perhaps with the state’s<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/11/06/illinois-house-speaker-chris-welch-steps-down-female-replacement-contenders" > first female legislative leader</a>? Women make up the vast majority of the House Democratic caucus, after all.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-3b0000" name="module-3b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>Buckner has also been one of Welch’s go-to members to tackle big projects, like the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fran-spielman-show/2026/05/29/state-rep-kam-buckner-bears-stadium-megaprojects-bill-arlington-heights-northwest-indiana-illinois-general-assembly" >Bears stadium</a> deal and mass transit reform and funding.</p><p>Buckner did put in a lot of work with other legislators, but his bills never made it to the governor’s desk. The Senate <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/31/bears-stadium-bill-springfield-arlington-heights-hammond-indiana" >refused to vote</a> on his Bears bill, and his transit bill’s funding sources were rejected by the Senate and the governor. Gov. JB Pritzker finally intervened with a somewhat “painless” funding plan that was eagerly passed by both chambers.</p><p>But then Buckner released a 15-point plan last week about how he would govern if elected House speaker. My associate Isabel Miller wrote about it for our subscribers, and I was quite impressed with the thought and care Buckner put into his proposal.</p><p>To be clear, I’m not in any way endorsing Buckner’s candidacy. That’s up to the House. But I do strongly believe that many if not all of his ideas ought to be incorporated or at least addressed by whomever does win the top job.</p><p>“The speaker’s first job is not to accumulate power, but to share it,” Buckner told colleagues in his email. What a novel and encouraging concept that is.</p><p>More from Isabel’s story:</p><p>“On legislation, Buckner wants policy development, negotiations and oversight moved back into standing committees, reducing reliance on working groups. Subcommittees would gain explicit authority to hold hearings, examine legislation and formally recommend action to their parent committees.”</p><p>The working groups have gotten way out of hand. They do all their work in private, rarely involve the Senate and the governor’s office and members tend to wait until the last minute to unveil their final project, when it’s too late for the other chamber to weigh in.</p><p>“The plan would give deputy House majority leaders specific assignments, such as labor, infrastructure or education, with authority and responsibilities beyond their titles. Buckner also wants stronger independent House budget analysis; revenue forecasting; policy research and oversight, including a return to adopting legislative revenue estimates — lawmakers’ assessment of how much money is available to spend.</p><p>“As he has said before, Buckner would eliminate the internal 60-vote rule, which requires sponsors to demonstrate enough support to pass legislation before it reaches the floor. That would not guarantee every bill a vote. Buckner says members would remain responsible for building support, while the speaker would have to explain why a bill could not advance and identify a path forward when one exists.</p><p>“’No member should spend weeks working a roll call for legislation that leadership has already determined will not advance,’” he wrote.</p><h3>More proposals for change</h3><p>Buckner also wants to establish a procedure for removing a member from the Democratic caucus. Welch abruptly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2025/05/16/emanuel-chris-welch-fred-crespo-ouster-house-commitee-seperate-budget-rich-mller" >kicked</a> state Rep. Fred Crespo, D-Hoffman Estates, out of the caucus for using House resources to develop some alternative budget ideas — many of which Welch and the other leaders used to balance the budget.</p><p>“Technology upgrades would include a member app, bill tracking, digital documents and automated notifications. Members would receive communications plans tailored to their districts, with regional media expertise and help with local newspapers, digital content and op-eds,” Isabel wrote.</p><p>The House Democrats are far behind in all of those areas, mainly because of lack of funding and imagination.</p><p>And Buckner would change the way staff complaints against members are handled, which was one of the straws that broke the camel’s back with Welch. He wants protections for whistleblowers, clear workplace standards and independent reporting channels, some of which he details in his letter.</p><p>There’s lots more, so I encourage you to follow this link: <a class="Link" href="https://49h7k5kab.cc.rs6.net/tn.jsp?f=001QFL8IIP9y3nwbSofWDeWov-jVbHnxvCzl3tzu-hLe-f6KLB7ZFdMq-SGDL5sVSGpBULjXEZ_jhYfeuEWX93B5iT-LnYimIEse_bIjQA-Xp9rlMH0kPJrX445O9FPNyNnJa-rV3XZ04MfwksI4i6Jig==&c=vWuW_0k2vJ4Cnt5RRHTrtucPcWsjehMnPEh8kwSVhbwIFdI2VYAvoA==&ch=sRL9OIl89a3C5NZ7xnURo-SqDpr3l5Qu_Un501s-AvrNeViVYA6ryA==" target="_blank" >shorturl.at/jDGU6</a></p><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-360000" name="module-360000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Third man arrested, charged in 2025 Belmont Cragin fatal stabbing
entries.summary: <p>A 21-year-old man was charged in connection with a fatal stabbing in the Belmont Cragin neighborhood last year, Chicago police said.</p><p>Emmanuel Martinez was arrested Wednesday in the 10200 block of South 76th Avenue and charged on three felony counts of murder and a single count of mob action involving force by two or more people, according to a police news release.</p><p>Martinez was identified as a suspect in the June 7, 2025 stabbing death of Yahir Viveros-Alarcon, 27, in the 5600 block of West Fullerton Avenue, police said.</p><p>Martinez is the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/11/second-man-charged-in-fatal-belmont-cragin-stabbing" target="_blank" >third suspect arrested </a>in the killing, including Jose Ramos, 25, who was charged with first-degree murder and mob action on Nov. 11, along with Sergio Vargas, 29, apprehended and charged on the same counts in November 2025.</p>

entries.title: Josh Giddey at point guard? This experiment is not going to end well
entries.summary: <p>So, here we are.</p><p>At the intersection between the small difference between experiment and theory. The Josh Giddey crossroads. Where drama surrounding his existence in a Bulls uniform is beginning to metastasize.</p><p>Experiments, if given the chance, should, by nature, be given the chance to be and end wrong. That doesn’t mean they are wrong; it just means a different or other route needs to be taken to get to the conclusion sought. To make the experiment not become an enigma.</p><p>Giddey running the point for the Bulls is an experiment. Year 3 is so far proving to be his Stage 5, the ‘‘Analyze Data and Draw Conclusion’’ part. The precursor to (the Bulls) facing a conclusion. Even as his 18-point, 14-rebound, nine-assist, four-turnover ‘‘bounce-back from the fourth quarter benching’’ game Wednesday showed the type of player Giddey needs to be for the Bulls to discover whom they can become, the inconsistency and unknowing of when another game like that will happen is equivalent of Giddey not saving himself from himself.</p><p>A CHGO Sports podcast clamped down on Giddey like Payton Pritchard in the Boston game and targeted him like most defenses seem to be doing whenever he has the rock: ‘‘The effort, the compete level was not there in a way it needed to be.’’ ‘‘It’s never good when my starting point guard in the fourth quarter of a game is unplayable.’’ ‘‘Is this guy good enough to lead your team when you’re playing at the highest level? From what I’ve seen this year . . . I don’t see it.’’ ‘‘I would like a real point guard on my team, please.’’</p><p>Between Matt Peck, Will Gottlieb and Big Dave Watson, the theory of Giddey was on full blast. ESPN apparently (according to Bulls Central) didn’t help by saying Giddey was (possibly) not in executive vice president Bryson Graham’s plan and instigating the term ‘‘bridge player’’ into his situation.</p><p>Of the fourth quarter benching, Giddey’s ‘‘ . . . that’s a point guard’s job. If I can’t do that, I probably shouldn’t be a point guard’’ comments he made about himself Monday that got points for his 100% realness somehow missed the credit that should have come with it for being the truth. As he may hold the answer to the conclusion of his own experiment.</p><p>The theory is that it’s the turnovers. It’s not just the turnovers; it’s more than that. Through the games so far that have made up this Bulls season, Giddey has fallen below his career ‘‘C-level’’ averages in other areas: field-goal and three-point percentages down, free-throw percentage way down, win shares down to below the fault line (-0.1), points and rebounds down, PER down.</p><p>All of which, when you compare his turnover average this season with his career average (3.3 versus 2.9), doesn’t come off as drastic as the conversation seems to be making it out to be.</p><p>Still, here we are.</p><p>The why of this trial (and error) run is a different piece of rhetoric. One that falls under the same ominous cloud as the Noa Essengue Experiment, the Patrick Williams Experiment, last season’s draft-deadline experiment — which included the horrific four-game, two-month Jaden Ivey Experiment and the miserably failed Ayo Dosunmu Experiment the Bulls decided to end before completion — if they fail to play this smart.</p><p>Like scientists instead of coaches and executives.</p><p>What cannot be overlooked, overstated enough or misunderstood in any way in this is the role playing alongside Coby White and Dosunmu had on Giddey’s play at the point during their tenures here. While Giddey ran the point during the last two seasons, the full responsibility of doing it was never all on him. Now it is. Which is a whole other ballgame.</p><p>Uncomfortable is what he is, theoretically. What he has been inside this experiment. The Bulls are forcing him to be something he’s not. Like the Bears did Devin Hester at wide receiver. It’s not that Giddey can’t play point, he just hasn’t found the way to do it without losing his entire style of play and the benefits that come with that. He also has not yet found anyone to lead him the right way into that transition. Which is coming at both the team’s and his expense.</p><p>Maybe he should call Ty Jerome and ask what’s the secret. A visit to the NBA psychological alchemist Iren Rainey, maybe?</p><p>An improbable half-court, game-ending, buzzer-beater in 2025 at the UC to beat the LeBron/Luka-led Lakers that will go down as his career promise. A shot by Giddey that, at the time, was believed (or desperately taken) to be the beginning of the Bulls’ return to (any) meaningful basketball-related conversation.</p><p>What was lost in his 25-point, 14-rebound, 11-assist performance that night against the Lakers were the seven turnovers he accumulated running the offense. From there, it has been — or seems to have been — a slow, inconsistent decline for Giddey since.</p><p>The jagged big pill that now must be swallowed: The Josh Giddey Experiment is an experiment gone wrong. He’s not wrong (as a player), the Bulls aren’t wrong (as a team for experimenting), he’s just the wrong player to be the orchestrator of this symphony. They both know they need to realign their whole line of thinking.</p><p>Yet, here we are.</p>

entries.title: Bulls fall in NBA Cup pool play but added a new starter to the lineup
entries.summary: <p>On a night when the Bulls were finally able to move Nic Claxton into the starting lineup, inching closer to being whole, the visiting Wizards already had a foundation piece in the middle of their lineup.</p><p>And unfortunately for the home team, Anthony Davis wasn’t on any sort of minutes restriction.</p><p>That was bad news for the Bulls, as Davis went off for 36 points and 11 rebounds, giving Washington the 98-94 win in an important Group C pool play game for the NBA Cup.</p><p>The bad taste to come out of the loss, however, wasn’t just what Davis did, but what the Bulls (4-11) didn’t do. Specifically, blowing a first-half lead by scoring just nine third-quarter points and still having a chance to take the lead with 21.8 seconds left in the game off a Claxton rebound.</p><p>The ball found its way into Norman Powell’s hands, who at first looked to have the space for a three down 96-94, but rather than try and play hero, drove the lane for his patented floater, only to watch it rim out and into the hands of Wizards veteran Khris Middleton with 6.3 seconds left.</p><p>“I liked the matchup I had, attack the paint,” Powell said of the play. “I saw Trae (Young) close on me super hard but I didn’t want to foul bait. I saw the drive and took the floater I’ve been taking since I was a kid. Just in and out.”</p><p>Which also dropped the Bulls to 1-2 in pool play, all but ending any hopes of capturing a wildcard.</p><p>As for the bigger picture, Claxton is likely headed for the starting lineup on a permanent basis, scoring 11 points and grabbing seven rebounds.</p><p>Acquired in a four-team trade back in July, Claxton suffered a hamstring injury right before fall camp started and was laid up through the first eight games of the regular season. He finally made his Bulls debut off the bench, and of course with minutes restrictions, two weeks ago against the 76ers.</p><p>With Jalen Smith a scratch Friday morning because of an illness, Claxton was the obvious choice to jump into the starting lineup.</p><p></p><p><b>Cup runneth over</b></p><p></p><p>The NBA Cup hasn’t been every coach’s cup of tea, especially the idea of point differential being a decider in the tiebreaker and that leading to some scores being run up at times.</p><p>Coach Tiago Splitter, however, was admittedly a fan of the in-season tournament.</p><p>“I like it, I really do,” Splitter said. “Right now people don’t give it the attention as far as what it means, but I think in the future it could be a bigger and bigger tournament.”</p><p></p><p><b>In the eyes</b></p><p></p><p>Caleb Wilson admitted on Friday that he was a believer in visualization, so the idea that he gets to sit on the bench while his hand heals and put himself into different actions and positions can only help his game.</p><p>“Every situation you’ve got to put yourself in the shoes of the situation that’s happening so of course I put myself in the shoes of, ‘Hey that was a nice move,’ or ‘I like what you did there,’ “ Wilson said. “I can put it in my repertoire. Most of the game is mental.”</p><p></p><p><b>Staying power</b></p><p></p><p>Noa Essengue played one of his better halves against the Wizards, scoring eight points. But the key was limiting his fouls. The second-year forward had just one going into the halftime locker room. Splitter credited a lot of film for Essengue.</p><p>“He knows, he understands,” Splitter said. “When you watch film with him he says the right things. It’s a matter of time, a matter of how many games is he going to need to know this and get better?”</p>

entries.title: Could a redevelopment authority solve Cook County's vacant lot problem?
entries.summary: <p>A group of Chicago leaders recently came up with some ideas for repurposing the estimated 50,000 vacant lots scattered across Cook County: an Englewood tree ribbon, community farms and gardens and new housing near South Chicago’s quantum computing campus.</p><p>The proposals were part of a series of workshops, or so-called charrettes, where participants such as developers, funders, artists and more discussed possible solutions for the thousands of vacant lots in the county. Their ideas were presented at the Chicago Architecture Center last month at an event called “The Future is on the Map.”</p><p>The charrettes hosted 175 leaders from around the Chicago area at the Obama Presidential Center in September to discuss three areas that the vacant lots could support: arts, culture and open space; housing; and economic development. Attendees included Chicago Transit Authority Acting President Nora Leerhsen and Michael Fassnacht, Clayco's chief growth officer and former CEO of World Business Chicago.</p><p>Ghian Foreman, president and CEO of the Emerald South Economic Development Collaborative and an attendee, said they came up with fresh ideas that included a range of perspectives.</p><p>“It was Chicago. It wasn't just the same people that I'm used to being in the room with saying the same things that we always say to each other,” Foreman said. “You had a cross-section of people across the city of Chicago, and everyone was able to put in a little bit of their expertise — like a potluck dinner. Everybody brought these ideas to the table.”</p><p>Also among the ideas was something that’s been floated in Chicago throughout the years: a redevelopment authority.</p><p>There are hundreds of redevelopment authorities across the U.S. At one point, there were 400 in <a class="Link" href="https://dof.ca.gov/programs/redevelopment/" target="_blank" ><u>California</u></a>. The public agencies operate at either the local, county or state level and are tasked with acquiring and priming land for redevelopment as a way to reduce community blight. But no redevelopment authorities exist in Illinois, according to Cook County Commissioner Bridget Gainer.</p><p>“If you look around, whether it's the city, the county, or the state, there is not one single entity that is responsible for producing housing at speed, at affordability and geographically distributed in communities all over,” Gainer said.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/12/15/24000161/cook-county-land-bank-authority-mustafaa-saleh-scam-fraud-sentence" >Cook County Land Bank Authority</a> was formed by the Cook County Board in 2013 to redevelop the large number of vacant properties in the county, from residential to commercial and industrial buildings. While the land bank has helped create roughly 3,000 homes, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/03/06/cook-county-board-commissioners-meeting-attendance-absence-stanley-moore-bridget-gainer" >Gainer</a> said it has a narrow scope for how it addresses vacancies and build new homes. As the state carves out agencies like the Northern Illinois Transit Authority, Gainer sees an opportunity to do something similar with housing.</p><p>Now, Gainer wants to lead the path to creating a redevelopment authority.</p><p>“The affordability of housing — it keeps people here. It grows our population. It allows people to have a dignified existence,” Gainer, who helped found the land bank, said. “It really behooves us to go out of our way to make it work.”</p><h3>More planning</h3><p>The Chicago region is just one place that has renewed interest in establishing redevelopment authorities. But interest in them is far and wide, said Justin Marlowe, director of the Center for Municipal Finance at the University of Chicago’s Harris School of Public Policy. He said it stems, in part, from the federal government <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/10/01/housing-action-illinois-sues-hud-trump-administration-nonprofit-radical-left-ngo" >pulling back funding</a> for the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.</p><p>“We typically thought about these sorts of redevelopment activities as having a lot of federal involvement, which is not to say that they don't or that they won't going forward,” Marlowe said. “But I think there's lots of questions right now about what kind of partner the federal government is going to be when it comes to these sorts of urban development issues. And so you have lots of places now saying if we're going to do this, we probably do need to muster the support to do it locally and regionally.”</p><p>Chicago owns <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/sites/block-builder/home/city-owned-land-inventory.html" target="_blank" >10,000 vacant lots</a> and has taken several stabs at reducing that figure, including launching the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/04/03/chicago-missing-middle-program-families-south-west-sides-vacant-lot" >Missing Middle Infill Housing</a> program in 2024. The program, which sells vacant land to developers for $1, has created more than 300 new homes on the South and West sides, where vacant lots are the most prolific.</p><p>A redevelopment authority could advance the city's work and the land bank's efforts by putting tax entitlement clearance, debt writing capacity and development authority under one entity, Gainer said.</p><div href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2025/12/24/obama-foundation-emerald-south-shared-vendor-network" >economic development</a> partner, aims to attract and coordinate investment in neighborhoods such as Washington Park, Woodlawn and South Shore, with a focus on increasing local ownership and prosperity. Its $50 million Terra Firma program is designed to beautify, maintain and activate vacant land.</p><p>Foreman said a redevelopment authority could help Emerald South flip those vacant lots by cutting through red tape, such as coordinating with different agencies and levels of authority from the Chicago Department of Planning and Development to the Department of Water Management, Cook County Land Bank and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/05/chicago-voter-vacancy-tax-fund-chicago-public-schools" >Chicago Public Schools</a>.</p><p>“One of our biggest challenges is we have so many different steps you have to go through and different sets of rules and competing priorities,” Foreman said. “How do we set these things up where we can be as efficient as possible? What would it look like to empower a group that could work across the [government agencies] to be able to get us what we're all looking for, which is the most efficient and effective way of improving our communities equally across the city, across the county, across the state? Ultimately, what we're looking for is improvement in the communities.”</p><p>Gainer said a redevelopment authority that mirrors NITA, serving a broad region, would make the most sense. </p><p>What’s next is a more focused planning process that Gainer wants to keep collaborative, similar to the charrettes.</p><p>As the region thinks about what’s next, Marlowe said it’s important to learn from other municipalities while taking a local approach — including how such an agency would be funded and how it’d track success.</p><p>“One of the things that we know from other places is these [agencies] work really well when they have very clear metrics for what success looks like, whether that's dollars of reinvestment, numbers of units of housing built, numbers of vacant lots cleared,” Marlowe said. “When you go to the regional level, the needs are going to be very different from one place to the next, and therefore, the metrics probably need to be different. So, how do [you] deal with that trade off? How do you deal with that complexity? I think it can be dealt with. It's just that you have to be very thoughtful about it from the beginning.”</p>

entries.title: Should Chicago bring back gunshot-detection technology? Here's what you told us
entries.summary: <p>Voters have said they want Chicago to bring back gunshot detection technology like ShotSpotter. And the Chicago City Council is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/11/18/shotspotter-gunshot-detection-technology-council-mandate-mayor-brandon-johnson-police-crime" >pushing Mayor Brandon Johnson’s administration</a> to sign a contract to do so. We asked readers what they think the city should do. Here's what you told us, lightly edited for clarity:</p><p>"Yes, because you also get to the victims faster."<br><i>— Timothy J. Durkee</i></p><p>"No. I dug into the data, and it's really not worth it for the money. We could spend that money doing prevention work and save many more people and increase quality of life without being surveyed and dumping out money into a private corporation."<br><i>— Anna Carvlin</i></p><p>"If they want to save lives and lock up some criminals along the way, then yes."<br><i>— Ant LoBo</i></p><p>"Not really, it doesn't do anything until after the person has been shot. ... I would prefer real live cameras."<br><i>— Vivian James</i></p><p>"Given we have had it and taken it away, what are the before and after statistics about response time and arrest-conviction rate? Is there a reduction in fatalities? What other data can we find to demonstrate its value?"<br><i>— Zoe Elizabeth Rebecca</i></p><p>"If it saves one life, it is well worth it."<br><i>— Joe Gale</i></p><p>It provides "notification of loud exhaust backfire or shooting after the fact when damage already done and offenders are long gone once police arrive. Better to have preventive measures like ending poverty, keeping fathers together with their families, ensuring people get good education, helping mental health."<br><i>— David MacLennan</i></p><p>"Didn't work and the money can put more officers on the streets."<br><i>— Umar Miller</i></p><p>"Many times police can get to a location even before the dispatcher even sends any cars to the location. entries.title: Pump the brakes on CTA, Pace fossil-fuel bus purchases
entries.summary: <p>The newly created <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/10/23/cta-northern-illinois-transit-authority-public-transit-natalie-moore" >Northern Illinois Transit Authority</a> faces its first major test Dec. 10, when its board votes on a proposed 2027–2031 <a class="Link" href="https://nita.illinois.gov/uploads/files/general/Transit-Funding/2027/NITA-Proposed-Budget-Book.pdf" target="_blank" >Five-Year Capital Program</a>. Right now, that capital plan is on a collision course with Illinois law.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/2/22/22945636/cta-electric-bus-fleet-phase-in-2040" >CTA</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/1/19/24044200/pace-electric-bus-transit" >Pace</a> tell the public they are committed to achieving 100% zero-emission bus fleets by 2040. Yet both agencies are asking NITA to approve tens of millions of dollars to buy buses that burn fossil fuels and will stay on our streets well past 2040.</p><p>Even worse, those purchases appear to be illegal.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-870000" name="module-870000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Since 2021, the Chicago chapter of the <a class="Link" href="https://climaterealitychicago.com/" target="_blank" >Climate Reality Project</a> has urged the Chicago Transit Authority, Pace and the former Regional Transportation Authority to accelerate bus electrification. CTA’s diesel buses alone account for roughly <a class="Link" href="https://nita.illinois.gov/uploads/files/general/Drupal-Old/documents/aboutus/meeting_documents/02-17-22/4a_Public%20comments%20for%202-17-22.pdf" target="_blank" >3%</a> of all on-road vehicle greenhouse-gas emissions in Chicago. Frustrated by years of inaction, we drafted legislation that became Illinois law in 2023 to ban fossil-fuel bus contracts starting in mid-2026.</p><p>When lawmakers created NITA this year, they preserved and strengthened that mandate. Illinois law now <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/legislation/ILCS/details?MajorTopic=GOVERNMENT&Chapter=SPECIAL%20DISTRICTS&ActName=Northern%20Illinois%20Transit%20Authority%20Act.&ActID=984&ChapterID=15&ChapAct=70+ILCS+3615%2F&SeqStart=700000&SeqEnd=5399609" target="_blank" >states</a> plainly, “The Authority may not enter into a new contract to purchase a bus that is not a zero-emission bus for the purpose of a Service Board’s transit bus fleet.”</p><p>The math behind the law is simple. Transit buses operate for about 14 years. Any fossil-fuel bus ordered today will still be spewing exhaust in 2040.</p><p>Yet CTA is proposing to buy <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/11/21/cta-hybrid-bus-federal-grant" >150 diesel-electric hybrid buses</a> starting in 2027, compared to just 40 battery-electric buses. Calling a diesel hybrid part of a zero-emission fleet does not make it so. Diesel hybrids still burn fossil fuel and cut greenhouse-gas emissions by only 10% to 20% compared to conventional diesel. Meanwhile, CTA programs another $297 million for bus purchases without specifying what types or how many buses it plans to buy.</p><p>Pace’s capital plan contains a similar contradiction. Alongside $150 million for 99 battery-electric buses, Pace programs roughly $68 million for additional fossil-fuel buses — including compressed natural gas and hybrid models — without disclosing exact vehicle counts.</p><p>This isn’t just an environmental and legal failure; it is a costly financial mistake. Using industry fuel and maintenance benchmarks, we estimate that transitioning CTA and Pace to a fully electric fleet would save the region more than $110 million every year in operating costs.</p><p>CTA will likely blame its slow transition on limited federal funding. That excuse doesn’t hold up. In 2022, when the federal government <a class="Link" href="https://www.route-fifty.com/infrastructure/2022/08/feds-award-16b-speed-transition-electric-and-hydrogen-buses/375866/" target="_blank" >distributed $1.6 billion</a> for zero-emission buses and garages, transit agencies in New York, Boston and Los Angeles each won more than $100 million. CTA requested only $29 million for 10 electric buses and a minor garage upgrade because it hadn’t done the engineering work needed to compete for major infrastructure grants.</p><p>That lack of preparation is still crippling CTA’s garage electrification. CTA’s 2022 Charging Forward plan promised electric buses operating out of its 103rd Street Garage by 2024 and its 77th Street Garage by 2027. Today, CTA is only just requesting $133 million to retrofit 103rd Street — three years behind schedule — while omitting dedicated electrification funding for 77th Street, 74th Street and a planned West Side or South Side garage. Pace has been more proactive in Waukegan, Elgin and Wheeling, yet still hasn’t provided a transparent fleet schedule.</p><p>Taxpayers and riders created NITA to bring real oversight and accountability to regional transit. Allowing CTA and Pace to redefine “zero emissions” to include fossil-fuel buses — while hiding fleet numbers behind vague budget lines — would make a mockery of that reform.</p><p>Before voting Dec. 10, the NITA Board must send this capital plan back and demand three things: Remove every fossil-fuel bus purchase to comply with state law; publish exact, transparent procurement schedules for every bus dollar; and establish a funded, credible timeline to electrify CTA and Pace garages.</p><p>A zero-emission commitment must mean zero emissions from a bus tailpipe — not slightly lower emissions, not hybrid emissions and not promises that are contradicted by the buses being programmed in this five-year capital plan.</p><p>The NITA board should send these plans back for revision for a capital plan that complies with Illinois law and make a credible path to a truly zero-emission fleet by 2040. The planet and the people of Northeastern Illinois demand nothing less.</p><p><i>Bruce W. Mainzer is a former mass transit executive in Chicago and New York City and has also worked as a consultant in ground transport and other industries. He retired in 2019 and served as co-chair of the Chicago chapter of the Climate Reality Project between 2021 and 2025.</i> <br><i>.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ce0000" name="module-ce0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Helping Illinoisans navigate upcoming Medicaid changes
entries.summary: <p>Because of changes made in Washington, D.C., thousands of Illinois families could lose their Medicaid coverage next year — not because they stopped qualifying but because of new paperwork.</p><p>A federal law passed in July 2025 changes the rules in 2027 for adults covered through the Affordable Care Act expansion — generally people ages 19 to 64 who are not on Medicare. Instead of renewing their coverage once a year, they will have to renew every six months. Many will also eventually have to document about 80 hours a month of work, community service or school, unless they qualify for an exemption.</p><p>There is still time to soften the blow. Medicaid applications and renewals completed before 5 p.m. on Dec. 31 may lock in a full 12 months of coverage. That means a full year of stability before the new rules hit.</p><p>I am calling on our hospitals, community health centers and Medicaid health plans to act now. Screen uninsured patients. Remind every Medicaid patient about renewal at every visit. Host evening and weekend enrollment events. Help people gather their documents early, before the year-end rush.</p><p>When people lose coverage, they skip care, miss prescriptions and end up in the emergency room. Families suffer, and hospitals absorb the cost. Keeping people covered is better for everyone.</p><p>If you or a loved one has Medicaid, don't wait. Make sure Illinois Healthcare and Family Services has your current address and phone number, open every notice and renew, or apply at <a class="Link" href="http://abe.illinois.gov/" target="_blank" >abe.illinois.gov</a>. You can find more information at <a class="Link" href="http://medicaid.illinois.gov/" target="_blank" >Medicaid.illinois.gov</a>.</p><p>Washington made this harder. Here in Illinois, we can make sure no one loses their healthcare over paperwork.</p><p><i>State Rep. La Shawn K. Ford, D-Chicago</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-380000" name="module-380000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Mayoral candidates can learn from Colom victory</h3><p>After days of cliffhanger vote counts, Democrat Scott Colom became the first Black senator elected in Mississippi since Reconstruction, ending a nearly 150-year drought, as Arionne Nettles wrote in her <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/11/18/black-chicagoans-mississippi-midterms-scott-colom-reconstruction-arionne-nettles" >column </a>last week. </p><p>Capping a midterm cycle that expanded Black leadership nationwide, this breakthrough was driven by an urgent determination to protect the right to vote itself. In a state scarred by Jim Crow terror — from Emmett Till’s lynching to NAACP leader Medgar Evers’ assassination — Black voters turned out in record numbers despite fresh threats. Following the Supreme Court’s ruling in Louisiana v. Callais weakening the Voting Rights Act, aggressive registration sweeps using flawed consumer data mistakenly removed roughly 1 in 9 voters, forcing thousands onto provisional ballots and prolonging the count. Yet voters answered Colom’s call to honor those who died for the ballot.</p><p>For Chicagoans, that triumph in the Delta hits close to home, as Nettles pointed out. Hundreds of thousands of Black families rode the Illinois Central Railroad north during the Great Migration to Chicago’s South and West sides— building communities in Bronzeville, Chatham, Austin and Englewood — and bringing an organizing tradition that fueled Harold Washington’s 1983 coalition.</p><p>As Chicago prepares for a critical mayoral race with more than a dozen contenders vying for City Hall, candidates should take note. Divided roughly into thirds among Black, white and Latino residents, alongside a growing Asian American community, Chicago has a Black electorate representing a decisive third of the city. Too often, contenders court Black voters early, yet take their loyalty for granted, assuming voters will fall in line behind familiar names or endorsements without tangible results.</p><p>Winning the Fifth Floor requires confronting the economic and structural priorities of Black Chicagoans head-on. That begins with critical neighborhood investment and job creation — backing local entrepreneurs, revitalizing commercial corridors and connecting residents to good-paying careers rather than relying on Downtown megaprojects alone. It demands sustainable funding for neighborhood public schools and multilayered public safety strategies pairing root-cause investments with fair, accountable policing.</p><p>Mississippi reminded us that political power is built from the ground up. In a packed mayoral field, no candidate can afford to treat Black Chicagoans as an automatic vote. The unbroken line between the Delta and Lake Michigan remains discerning, organized and decisive.</p><p><i>Glenn Eden, former board chair, Choose Chicago</i></p><h3>Competence, not conflict</h3><p>Conflict is the intentional camouflage of incompetence. Donald Trump and his enablers in and and out of government have demonstrated this the last two years. They have no desire to govern, much less a plan to do so. Their so-called signature achievement — the One Big Beautiful Bill<b> </b>— wasn't governance. It was a giveaway to the super rich and giant corporations.</p><p>Now comes Trump's first major decision since the November midterms. And he gifts us with Stephen Miller as his chief of staff, a man whose cruelty birthed the outrageous abuses of the U.S. immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, trumped-up (pun intended) culture war skirmishes and thinly disguised misogyny. Conflict anyone?</p><p>Which informs my advice to our newly elected representatives. Don't engage. When the party of incompetence blathers on about transgender athletes, "woke" educators or socialized medicine, ignore them. Focus on meaningful governance. The overwhelming majority of voters want affordable housing, to halt the spread of oligarchy, substantial infrastructure investment, an end to the war in Iran, a solution for the student loan debt crisis, universal affordable healthcare, etc. We don't need more conflict. We need competence.</p><p><i>Mark Lipscomb, McKinley Park</i></p><h3>Trump’s self-obsession </h3><p>By constantly referencing his ballroom, arch and helipad instead of answering reporters' questions about Ukraine and the Iran war, it's becoming increasingly clear that the only person suffering from Trump Derangement Syndrome is our deranged president, Donald Trump.</p><p><i>Arthur S. Kazar, Forest Park</i> </p><h3>What would evangelicals do? </h3><p>If Jesus were running for president as a socialist democrat, would white, ultra-conservative evangelicals vote for him? Just wondering.</p><p><i>Wes Dickson, Orland Park</i> </p><h3>CTU, CPS Board: Put students first </h3><p>For over a decade, the Chicago Teachers Union pushed for a fully elected Chicago Public Schools board. On Nov. 3 it got one — and voters denied the union control.</p><p>Under former Mayors Rahm Emanuel and Lori Lightfoot, the appointed board was a battleground between CTU and City Hall. That changed when former CTU organizer Brandon Johnson became mayor and had the power to appoint a controlling majority of the hybrid board.</p><p>A fully elected board required the union to make its case directly to voters. For the second consecutive school board election, it fell short. In 2024, CTU poured <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinoispolicy.org/chicago-teachers-union-spends-2-1m-on-losing-school-board-candidates/" target="_blank" >$2.8 million</a> into board races and lost six of nine contested seats.</p><p>Now, CTU-endorsed candidates appear to have won just nine of 21 seats. Voters rejected its candidate for board president despite more than <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/11/06/chicago-school-board-ctu-teachers-union-spending" >$2.6 million</a> in campaign support from CTU and aligned organizations.</p><p>The new board should use that independence to improve academic achievement and bring accountability to district spending. That means asking whether each dollar improves the education students receive and whether district leaders are delivering the progress they promised to families.</p><p>Start with reading instruction grounded in proven methods, including the science of reading. Require specific improvement plans for the lowest-performing schools and hold district leaders accountable for carrying them out. They should also give families at high-performing charter schools certainty by renewing contracts at least six months before they expire.</p><p>On finances, move to zero-based budgeting by fiscal 2028, requiring every department and school to justify its spending. Commission an independent assessment of district facilities so decisions about near-empty buildings and staffing reflect students’ educational needs and enrollment realities.</p><p>Members should also ask Springfield to require a fiscal note and state prepayment for pension benefit increases that impose costs on local districts. Taxpayers deserve to know what those promises cost before lawmakers approve them.</p><p>These responsibilities will sometimes require board members to disagree with CTU. Every board member, regardless of endorsement, owes students and families that independent judgment.</p><p>The union fought for voters to have a say. The new board should honor their decision by putting students first.</p><p><i>Mailee Smith, vice president of policy and litigation, Illinois Policy Institute</i></p><h3>Honoring a Lithuanian American leader</h3><p>Valdas Adamkus, a longtime environmental leader in Chicago and later president of Lithuania, turned 100 on Nov. 3. I had the honor of being in Lithuania's capital, Vilnius, to attend the celebration of his life. The outpouring of love, respect and appreciation for what he has done for Lithuania was remarkable.</p><p>I gave a talk in the city of Kaunas the week before about Adamkus’ 27 years with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s Great Lakes Region. I worked with him for 25 of those years — five as his deputy. His career at the EPA was defined by integrity, honesty, courage and a steady moral compass. He was a champion for the Great Lakes and fought for the rights of Indigenous people in the region. He faced down some of the biggest corporations, including Dow, Outboard Marine Corp. and U.S. Steel, and made them clean up. A pristine river in Northern Michigan is now part of a national park because he objected to plans by a developer to build a golf course on its shores.</p><p>When political pressure was exerted from Washington, D.C., Adamkus always stood up for the environment. In his early 70s, he returned to Lithuania and was elected president for two terms. He led the country into NATO, the European Union and a democratic future. Many countries have awarded him high honors, and colleges and universities have granted him honorary doctorates. Stephanie Zimmermann's Sun-Times <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-history/2026/07/25/president-valdas-adamkus-lithuania-100-interview-biography-chicago-connection" target="_blank" >story</a> on Adamkus and her series on Lithuania over the summer highlighted many of his accomplishments. At a time of so much turmoil in the world, we need many more leaders like Adamkus.</p><p><i>David A. Ullrich, Lake View</i></p><h3>Save animals from contest cruelty</h3><p>As a Chicagoan who cares about protecting wildlife, I find it disturbing that Illinois still allows contests in which wild animals are killed for cash prizes and recognition.</p><p>Coyotes, foxes and other wild animals are an important part of our natural environment. They play a valuable role in maintaining healthy ecosystems and deserve to be treated with respect, not reduced to trophies.</p><p>There is a fundamental difference between lawful hunting and killing animals for contests. Rewarding participants for killing the most, largest or smallest animals sends the wrong message about how we value wildlife.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://legiscan.com/IL/text/SB3063/id/3341647" target="_blank" >Senate Bill 3063</a> would prohibit prize-based killing contests involving fur-bearing mammals while preserving otherwise lawful hunting and trapping. This is a reasonable and compassionate step toward better wildlife protection in Illinois.</p><p>I urge Illinois Senate President Don Harmon to ensure that SB 3063 is assigned to a substantive committee for a hearing.</p><p>Illinois has an opportunity to demonstrate that wildlife is worth protecting, not exploiting for prizes. Our state can and should do better.</p><p><i>Abbie Jacobson, Logan Square</i></p><h3>Don’t let arrest distract from animal abuse </h3><p>I wanted to comment on the recent Sun-Times <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/11/18/chicago-animal-rights-activist-sentenced-jail-time-after-falsely-reporting-shooting-at-backyard-rodeo-shark-ogle-county" >story</a> headlined, “Chicago animal rights activist is sentenced to jail time after falsely reporting shooting at backyard rodeo"</p><p>Jodie Wiederkehr’s mistake should not distract from the reason animal advocates were at the rodeo in the first place: Animals were being subjected to a spectacle in which steers are chased down and deliberately toppled by their tails, a practice that can result in horrific injuries, including the skin and tissue of the tail being torn from their body.</p><p>It’s unacceptable that anyone should have to plead with authorities to take such cruelty seriously. We should be asking why inflicting terror, pain and potentially catastrophic injuries on animals continues to be tolerated.</p><p>Rather than allowing one activist’s lapse in judgment to become the entire story, Illinois officials should address the cruelty that prompted the protests in the first place and make it unmistakably clear that tormenting animals has no place in a civilized society.</p><p><i>Jennifer O'Connor, senior writer, PETA Foundation</i><br></p>

entries.title: Bears-Saints: What To Watch For
entries.summary: <h3><b>WHEN THE BEARS HAVE THE BALL</b></h3><p>There was a time when Montez Sweat and Chase Young were the future of Washington’s franchise. In 2020, Sweat led the team with nine sacks, while Young, the rookie picked No. 2 overall, had 7 ½.</p><p>The next year, the two combined to miss 15 games. The year after that, Young played in only three. In 2023, Washington traded both on the same day — Sweat to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> for a second-round pick and Young to the 49ers for a third-rounder.</p><p>Now with the Saints, Young is in the midst of his best season. He’s tied for fourth in the NFL with eight sacks. The defensive end on the other side of the line, Carl Granderson, has 8 ½.</p><p>A Saints defense that gives up the fourth-most yards and eighth-most points in the NFL knows how to rush the passer. They have 26 sacks, as many as the Bears do.</p><p>The Bears, though, are just as concerned about allowing pressure from blitzers up the middle as they are around the edge. The Buccaneers were successful with that approach, and so were the Vikings in Week 2. Those inside Halas Hall expect the rest of the league to attack the Bears the same way until they prove they can stop it.</p><p>With Kyle Monangai joining D’Andre Swift for the first time since Week 4, the Bears figure to run the ball to stay out of obvious third down passing situations. The Saints give up 75 rushing yards per game between the tackles, the most in the NFL.</p><h3><b>WHEN THE SAINTS HAVE THE BALL</b></h3><h3></h3><p>The Saints have a right tackle problem. Taliese Fuaga is out multiple weeks with a knee sprain. Last week, backup right tackle Asim Richards hurt his own knee. That leaves the Saints with Mason Murphy starting Sunday. The Bears know him well — the rookie spent all of training camp playing for Ben Johnson before became the only player the team waived on cut day to be claimed Aug. 31. He’s played just 17 offensive snaps over six games this season, being used more often on special teams downs.</p><p>That’s good news for whomever lines up over right tackle — most likely edge rusher Austin Booker, who had a sack and two quarterback hits against the Buccaneers in the Bears’ last game.</p><p>They have a hole at center, too — starter Erik McCoy was ruled out with a biceps problem.</p><p>Quarterback Tyler Shough will be under pressure, then, whether the Bears blitz or not. He’s faced a blitz on 79 dropbacks this season, the most in the NFL this season, per NFL Next Gen Stats. One-fifth of the time, he’s being blitzed by a defensive back. He’s taken eight sacks in those situations, the most in the NFL.</p><p>Pro Football Focus, though, gives him their sixth-highest grade when under pressure, one spot behind the Bears’ Caleb Williams.</p><p>The Bears were one of the most blitz-happy teams in the NFL before they traded for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. Since acquiring him, however, they’ve rushed four defenders three-quarters of the time.<br></p>

entries.summary: <p>This week’s top photo comes from photojournalist <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/tyler-pasciak-lariviere" target="_blank" >Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere</a>. Follow him on <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/TylerLaRiviere" target="_blank" >X</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://bsky.app/profile/tylerplariviere.bsky.social" target="_blank" >Blue Sky</a>, and <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/tylerpasciaklariviere/" target="_blank" >Instagram</a>.</p><h3>What makes this photo important?</h3><p>This image showcases a fraction of the human experience from the first nationwide ground stop in 25 years at one of the nation's busiest airports — pure stress, anxiety, and exhaustion felt by all those affected by the unexpected event.</p><h3>How I got this photo:</h3><p>While at Terminal 1 in O'hare International Airport, I was looking to capture images of any chaos caused by the unexpected ground stop. I was anticipating a scene of comically long lines and even a few overly frustrated people, but none of that was really happening. I decided to venture down to baggage claim to find that this was where much of the anticipated chaos was happening. As I wandered through the different claim areas, I saw many passengers waiting around, slews of bags continuously flooding out onto the carousels, all while employees were trying their best to keep everything orderly in spite of the situation. In my wandering, I noticed a group of young passengers who were laying on the ground, looking completely defeated from the situation. It was shortly after taking this photo that the Federal Aviation Administration announced the ground stop was over.</p><p></p><h3><b>Technical details:</b></h3><p></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-9460a7e0-1f16-11f1-ad7a-f35fc19f6d46" style="font-style: normal; font-variant-caps: normal; orphans: 2; text-align: start; text-indent: 0px; text-transform: none; white-space: normal; widows: 2; word-spacing: 0px; -webkit-text-stroke-width: 0px; text-decoration-line: none; text-decoration-thickness: auto; text-decoration-style: solid; background-repeat: no-repeat; box-sizing: border-box; margin: 0px 0px 0px 10px; padding: 0px 0px 0px 20px; list-style: outside; caret-color: rgb(42, 42, 42); color: rgb(42, 42, 42); font-family: Arial; font-size: 18px; font-weight: 300; letter-spacing: -0.018px; padding-inline-start: 48px;"><li>Equipment: Nikon Z9 with 24-70mm F/2.8 Lens</li><li>Focal length: 34mm</li><li>Aperture: F/6.3</li><li>Exposure: 1/500</li><li>ISO: 8000</li></ul><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/11/13/all-departing-flights-grounded-nationwide-due-to-faa-order" >FAA lifts nationwide ground stop. entries.title: Dear Abby: Near-sexagenarian still dreams of fatherhood
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am a 59-year-old male wheelchair user and survivor of Guillain-Barre syndrome, which struck me in 2023. I've never been married nor had kids. I'd still like to get married and have at least one child. Considering my age, I realize that if I have a kid at 61, the kid would be 10 when I'm 71, and so on. Would it be better not to have kids due to my age, or is it more moral and ethical to become a father while I can? — <i>DAD IN WAITING</i></p><p><b>DEAR DAD IN WAITING:</b> Unless your spiritual adviser insists otherwise, there's no moral imperative for you to have a child. For now, focus on your marriage goal by building a relationship. Do you have someone in mind? If your partner wants to have a child, discuss your concerns about your age before proceeding. To offset the age gap, you might consider adopting an older child. If you decide to follow through with either option, the two of you will need a childcare plan that accounts for your physical limitations and financial situation.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I recently visited my mother and her husband. It's a two-day drive. They have two small yapping dogs and one large yapping dog. The three animals have the run of the place. I get it; these are their beloved dogs. When I complained about the yapping and barking, I was told to "get over it." Am I wrong to hope they remove the dogs from rooms we inhabit, like the living room and kitchen? — <i>DOGS RULE IN CALIFORNIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR DOGS RULE:</b> Their house, their rules. You asked, and your request was denied. Instead of staying with the dogs while you visit, consider a nearby hotel or B&B. Invite your mom and stepdad out for a meal so you won't be subjected to the constant barking. If these options are too expensive, or if Mom won't cooperate, choose to see them less often. Much less.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My 25-year-old grandson has cut off all contact with his mother (my daughter). I can't say I blame him; she can be toxic, and his childhood was difficult. He left home on his 18th birthday and has since moved across the country. I am in regular contact with him. My daughter has grown some since he was a child and has been a better mother to her younger children, but the damage is done.</p><p>The problem is that she knows I know how to reach him, and she's desperate to reestablish contact with him. She's alternately angry or tearful, begging me to reveal his location. I can see both of their points of view. She says she loves him and wants a relationship; he does not. Am I right to honor my grandson's wishes at the expense of my daughter, whom I also love? — <i>TORN IN TWO</i></p><p><b>DEAR TORN:</b> This is your daughter's problem, not yours. Your grandson moved across the country for a reason. He wants nothing more to do with your toxic daughter (who has "grown some"). If you divulge his location, you will have betrayed his trust, and it's likely he will have nothing more to do with you. Don't do it!</p><p>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127. </p>

entries.title: 2 killed in West Town shooting
entries.summary: <p>A man and woman were fatally shot after an argument broke out early Saturday in West Town. </p><p>They were standing with a group in the 1000 block of North Milwaukee Avenue around 2 a.m. when an argument began with an unknown person, Chicago police said. </p><p>The person pulled out a gun and opened fire, police said. </p><p>The man suffered multiple gunshot wounds and the woman was struck in the chest. They were taken to Stroger Hospital and both were pronounced dead. </p><p>No arrests were made. </p>

entries.title: Third quarter woes continue for the Bulls and cost them against Wizards
entries.summary: <p>It felt like the third quarter calamity was in the rear-view mirror.</p><p>An early bump in the season that just needed to be ironed out.</p><p>All proven to be wrong on Friday, and Bulls veteran Norman Powell wasn’t shy about pointing out a pox on his team’s third-quarter mentality.</p><p>“We just got to figure it out,” Powell said. “I think it’s like the focus. I don’t know if we need to get out (of the locker room and onto the court) earlier and get our bodies moving or I don’t know, we just got to figure out how to come out with the same mentality we have to start the games in the first two quarters. We talk about it, but we can’t keep coming in here and that being the reason why we’re in closely contested games and we’re making it tough on ourselves later in games.”</p><p>That they did against the Wizards.</p><p>The Bulls went into halftime with a solid eight-point lead and by the time the third-quarter horn sounded they had scored just nine points, shot a miserable 3-for-25, and allowed 23 points. Sure, there was fight in the final stanza, but the damage was done. And not the first time this season by a longshot.</p><p>When Washington beat the Bulls earlier this season, a 40-20 third quarter was a big reason why. Then there was the Spurs game two weeks ago in which a great first half was quickly erased when the Bulls came out of the locker room and watched the Spurs go on a 34-19 run the next 12 minutes.</p><p>It felt like it was cleaned up since, but not the case.</p><p>“Third quarter, we’ve got to figure it out,” coach Tiago Splitter said. “We’ve got to start those quarters better. To only score nine points, do you have the same energy that you have the first half? We gotta get better.”</p><p>The overall numbers scream that.</p><p>The Bulls will enter the Sunday game with Denver averaging 26.3 points in the third, which is fifth worst in the league. Their 43.3% from the field is sixth worse, and the 30.7% from three-point range is third worst. Meanwhile, the plus/minus in the third is minus-5.3. Only the lowly Kings are worse at minus-5.9 in plus/minus in the third.</p><p>“These teams are good,” Powell said. “A 20-point lead can be eaten up pretty quick if you don’t have the right mindset with the way teams are shooting threes, attacking, stuff like that, so we just got to do a better job as a collective coming out with the right focus and mentality in the third.”</p><p>What didn’t help against the Wizards was a quick turnover by Josh Giddey and then a Matas Buzelis turnover on the first two second-half possessions. That wasn’t the only issue by any means, but both of those players eventually paid the price.</p><p>Both Giddey and Buzelis were all but benched in the fourth, getting less than four minutes of work and not thrilled with it afterward based on their body language. According to Splitter, however, it was that body language in the third that he didn’t love, leading to his decision.</p><p>“I thought they didn’t have a good game,” Splitter said of the two starters. “Those guys were having a bad night.</p><p>“I think one of the things is even if the shots aren’t falling you can still play the right way. I think that’s what happened; when you miss a couple shots and you’re not playing the right way. Again, learn from it and be in a better place next game.”</p><p>Powell hopes the entire team will be.</p><p>“(The Wizards) were the harder playing team coming out into that third quarter,” Powell added. “I liked how we stayed in it, took their punch and gave ourselves a chance to crawl back into the game, but we shot ourselves in the foot in that third.”</p>

entries.title: White Sox are setting up for a big offseason move, after quickly shedding past misfires
entries.summary: <p>The organizations he’s hired people away from were a hint, but White Sox general manager Chris Getz has been open about where his influences lie.</p><p>“I find it really fascinating when you've got the Tampa Bay Rays, the Milwaukee Brewers, the Cleveland Guardians that are at the top of their divisions on a regular basis,” Getz told me this spring.</p><p>He stipulated there are lessons to take from the Dodgers and Yankees as well, but the last two years of White Sox baseball have operated closer to the Brewers and Rays, both in terms of payroll and how transaction-heavy they have been.</p><p>Part of how those teams have remained competitive despite payroll limitations is an unhesitant, unsentimental approach to doing business, at least in terms of swinging trades and making moves. These clubs don’t feel they can afford to carry many high salaries, and err on the side of cutting ties too soon, rather than footing the bill for cutting ties too late.</p><p>The three greatest players in Rays history–Evan Longoria, Carl Crawford, Ben Zobrist–all played the bulk of their 30s elsewhere. Brewers manager Pat Murphy went viral for joking about NLCS MVP Jake Bauers’ imminent departure in free agency while confetti was literally still falling down on both of them. When assistant general manager Carlos Rodriguez–who spent 16 years with the Rays, of course–was first introduced to the media in February, I asked if he foresaw the White Sox adapting a similar wheeling-and-dealing nature.</p><p>Rodriguez mostly demurred on declaring the franchise’s approach during his second month on the job, but his answer is interesting to apply to the Sox’ most recent trade of Luis Castillo and Davis Martin to the Rockies for two middling prospects.</p><p>“If it means making a transaction that allows the organization and the team to be more competitive or add more wins, whether it’s this year, or in the future, those are shots we will hopefully be able to take,” Rodriguez said.</p><p>With apologies to left-hander Sean Sullivan’s deceptive delivery and Douglas Veliz’s encouraging Dominican Summer League stats, the trade the Sox pulled on Thursday night clearly didn’t add wins in a vacuum. The Sox wanted to dump Castillo’s salary upon the Rockies, and paid them the price of a very affordable, solid-average starter in Davis Martin to do it. The value of the trade will be defined by the future signings it enables, for a Sox team that wants to land impact starting pitching in the free-agent market, while staying within their budget.</p><p>Losing Martin’s clubhouse presence, a pitcher Getz discussed as someone he uniquely trusted for his insight on the team’s needs, is an intangible cost that’s hard to measure. But what Getz has really shown he won’t be sentimental toward is his own ideas.</p><p>Four months ago, Getz sold Castillo as a boon to the White Sox rotation despite 2026 numbers that were the worst of his career, and now has conceded it was necessary to move on. The deal to acquire Castillo was itself a concession that a two-year, $20 million free-agent contract to make Seranthony Dominguez their closer hadn’t worked, and dumping his contract on the Mariners was better than hoping for a turnaround. To go even further, Dominguez was acquired with money freed up when Luis Robert Jr. was traded to the Mets in a salary dump which conceded the Sox could no longer wait for a 2023 redux.</p><p>A pessimistic–but not unfair–view is digging out from under this string of misses have cost the Sox both Martin and an interesting power-hitting prospect in Boston Smith, who went to Seattle in the Castillo trade. A rosier outlook is to compare how the Sox roster would look if they refused to surrender on any of these projects, to this present reality where they look primed to try to redeem it all with potentially the biggest investment in a free-agent starting pitcher in franchise history.</p><p>The latter is a lot more compelling. It’s just that the skill of quickly pivoting off misses won’t be as useful for nailing this one.</p>

entries.title: Chicago reaches third warmest fall in 150 years, says National Weather Service
entries.summary: <p>The ongoing fall warm front in Chicago continues at a historic level. </p><p>The city is experiencing its third-warmest fall on record, according to National Weather Service after temperatures reached another milestone this weekend.</p><p>Friday's high of 68 degrees tied the record for Nov. 20 set in 1930, Gino. Temperatures climbed to 69 degrees Saturday before a cooling expected to begin Sunday.</p><p>Only 1931 and 2024 have been warmer since the agency began keeping records more than 155 years ago.</p><p>The unseasonably warm stretch may be <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/11/20/unseasonably-warm-temperatures-may-break-nearly-century-old-record-high" target="_blank" >linked to strong El Niño conditions</a> this year, according to Kevin Birk, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Chicago.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/10/23/after-a-year-of-unusual-weather-in-chicago-should-you-brace-for-winter" target="_blank" >El Niño</a> is a climate pattern characterized by unusually warm ocean temperatures in the Pacific Ocean that can influence weather patterns around the world. </p><p>In September, the <a class="Link" href="https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/el-nino-set-become-very-strong-raising-risks-of-extreme-weather-2027" target="_blank" >World Meteological Organization</a> forecast that El Niño conditions could become “very strong,” increasing the risk of extreme weather through February 2027.<br></p>
